questions.prompt: Find the error: "She is going to becomes a translator."

options.text: She is
going to
a translator
becomes

questions.explanation: The error is "becomes": after going to, the verb stays in its base form for every subject — She is going to become a translator. The -s belongs to the simple present, not to be going to. "She is" and "going to" are correct for she, and "a translator" is the right object.

options.text: I'm thinking to leave school.
I'm thinking of leave school.
I'm thinking of leaving school.
I'm thinking of to leave school.

questions.explanation: be thinking of + verb + ing: I'm thinking of leaving school, because after the preposition "of" the verb takes -ing. "thinking to leave" borrows the "to" of intend to; "of leave" forgets the -ing; "of to leave" mixes the two structures.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a PLANNED ACTION, not an intention?

options.text: We are going to travel to Spain.
We are going to Spain after the exams.
We are going to buy tickets for Spain.
We are going to learn Spanish.

questions.explanation: In "We are going to Spain after the exams", no base verb follows going to — only a place: it is the verb go in the present progressive + a future word (after the exams), so a planned action. In the other three sentences, going to is followed by a base verb (travel, buy, learn): they express intentions.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a question: cost / will / how much / these cars

options.text: How much these cars will cost?
How much will cost these cars?
How much will these cars cost?
How much will these cars costs?

questions.explanation: A question in the future tense is will + subject + bare infinitive, after the question word: How much will these cars cost? "these cars will cost" keeps the order of a statement; "will cost these cars" puts the verb before the subject; "costs" adds -s after will, which never happens.

questions.prompt: Complete the negative: "Kate ___ tell her parents about her plan."

options.text: doesn't intend to
don't intend to
doesn't intends to
isn't intend to

questions.explanation: intend makes its negative with do / does, like any verb in the present; with Kate (she) it is doesn't, and the -s moves to does: Kate doesn't intend to tell her parents. "don't" is for I / you / we / they; "doesn't intends" keeps the -s twice; "isn't intend" uses be with an ordinary verb.

questions.prompt: Turn this planned action into an intention: "Peter is reviewing for his exam next week."

options.text: Peter going to review for his exam.
Peter is going to reviewing for his exam.
Peter will reviewing for his exam.
Peter is going to review for his exam.

questions.explanation: An intention is am / is / are + going to + base verb: Peter is going to review for his exam. "Peter going to review" drops "is"; "is going to reviewing" adds -ing where the base verb is needed; "will reviewing" puts -ing after will.
